bib.title: Achieving Peak Performance for Large Language Models: A Systematic Review

question: Which optimization and acceleration techniques, frameworks and libraries exist for LLM training, inference and serving (2017 to Dec 2023), and how do they compare on performance, cost and scalability?
contributions: Overview of language-model development and of commonly used frameworks and libraries (Tables 3 and 4).
Taxonomy of optimization strategies in three classes: training optimization, hardware optimization, scalability and reliability (Fig 1).
Comparative analysis of strategies on performance, cost and scalability (Tables 5, 6, 7).
Two case studies: SparseGPT for training-side size reduction, QMoE for inference efficiency.
Future directions for efficiency, scalability and flexibility.

results.claim: The review screened 983 records from five databases and included 65 studies (PRISMA).
results.setup: Systematic literature review, 2017 to December 2023, queries on LLM acceleration/optimization (Table 1), databases IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, Scopus, ResearchRabbit, arXiv.
results.quote: We reviewed 65 publications out of 983 from 2017 to December 2023, retrieved from 5 databases.
results.note: Fig 2 gives duplicates removed n = 41 and records screened n = 940; the text says the last search was 25 May 2024 although the window ends December 2023.

results.claim: Splitwise separates compute-bound prompt processing from memory-bound token generation onto different machines.
results.metric: throughput at equal or lower cost
results.value: up to 1.4x throughput at 20% lower cost, or 2.35x throughput at same cost and power
results.setup: As summarised by the survey; hardware and baseline systems are not stated in this paper.
results.quote: The model achieves up to 1.4× higher throughput at 20% lower cost or 2.35× higher throughput with the same cost and power consumption.

results.claim: vLLM with PagedAttention raises serving throughput by 2-4x over existing systems.
results.setup: Best for long sequences, large models and complex decoding algorithms; baselines not named in this paper.
results.quote: Evaluations present vLLM significantly improves throughput by 2-4× faster compared to existing systems

results.claim: PowerInfer runs LLMs on a consumer GPU by keeping frequently activated (hot) neurons on GPU and input-specific (cold) neurons on CPU.
results.value: up to 11.69x; 13.20 tokens per second average
results.quote: achieves inference speeds up to 11.69× faster inference than systems like llama.cpp.It delivers an average token generation rate of 13.20 tokens per second
results.note: Text line break splits the sentence; value also in Table 4.

results.claim: FlexGen offloading gives large throughput gains for OPT-175B on one T4 at the cost of latency in the thousands of seconds.
results.setup: Single T4 16 GB, 208 GB CPU DRAM, 1.5 TB SSD, input length 512, output length 32, OPT-175B.
results.quote: surpasses DeepSpeed Zero-Inference (batch size 1) by over 40×
results.note: The larger-batch figure is printed as 69x in Sec IV-B2 text and as 79x in Table 4, Table 6 (batch 256, 12000 s). The 100x figure uses 4-bit compression at 4000 s.

results.claim: DeepSpeed Inference raises throughput and cuts latency versus earlier systems and runs models 25x larger than GPU-only.
results.value: throughput more than 1.5x, latency more than 7.3x lower
results.setup: Throughput-oriented and latency-oriented scenarios respectively; 84 TFLOPS on A6000 for the 25x larger models.
results.quote: DeepSpeed Inference boosts throughput by more than 1.5× for throughput-oriented scenarios and minimizes the latency by more than 7.3×

results.claim: QMoE compresses a trillion-parameter MoE below 1 bit per parameter with under 5% runtime overhead.
results.value: 3.2 TB bfloat16 to under 160 GB (about 0.8 bits per parameter, 20x); overhead below 5%
results.setup: Runs on 4x NVIDIA A6000 or 8x NVIDIA RTX 3090; compression takes about a day on a single GPU; no retraining.
results.quote: QMoE can compress the SwitchTransformer-c2048 model to under 160 GB (20× compression, 0.8 bits per parameter) with minimal impact on accuracy
results.note: Case study (Sec VIII-B) also says size reduced by approximately 95%; accuracy numbers are not given.

results.claim: SparseGPT prunes OPT-175B and BLOOM-176B to 50-60% unstructured sparsity in one shot with negligible perplexity increase.
results.setup: OPT-175B and BLOOM-176B, post-training, no retraining; larger models prune more easily.
results.quote: It makes the model achieve 50-60% unstructured sparsity with a negligible increase in perplexity and removes more than 100 billion weights with minimal impact on accuracy.

results.claim: GPTQ quantizes models with hundreds of billions of parameters to 3-4 bits in about 4 GPU hours with minimal accuracy loss.
results.value: about 4 GPU hours; up to 3.25x on A100 and 4.5x on A6000 over FP16
results.setup: OPT-175B and BLOOM-176B, 3 or 4 bits per weight.
results.quote: it took approximately 4 GPU hours by reducing the bitwidth down to 3 or 4 bits per weight
results.note: The speedup sentence is garbled in the survey (reads '4.5x and up to 4.5x').

results.claim: FP8 mixed-precision training of GPT-175B cuts memory and raises speed versus BF16.
results.metric: memory reduction and training speed vs BF16
results.setup: GPT-175B on H100 GPUs; 37% faster than NVIDIA Transformer Engine.
results.quote: the FP8 framework reduced memory usage by 39% and increased training speed by 75% compared to the BF16 framework

results.claim: LLM-Pruner retains about 95% of performance after structural pruning of 20% of parameters; higher rates degrade sharply.
results.setup: LLaMA, Vicuna, ChatGLM; LoRA recovery tuning with 50K samples in 3 hours.
results.quote: the compressed models maintain 94.97% of their original performance even after removing 20% of parameters

results.claim: Eliseev and Mazur run Mixtral-8x7B on consumer hardware by MoE-specific expert offloading (LRU cache plus expert prediction).
results.setup: Mixtral-8x7B with mixed quantization on consumer GPUs and free-tier Google Colab.
results.quote: achieving 2-3 tokens per second on various consumer GPUs

results.claim: Sheared LLaMA prunes LLaMA2-7B to 1.3B and 2.7B using about 3% of the compute of training those sizes from scratch.
results.quote: LLM-shearing also requires only 3% of the computing resources to train as the same models trained from scratch.

results.claim: LoRA cuts trainable parameters by 10,000x and GPU memory by 3x versus Adam fine-tuning of GPT-3 175B.
results.setup: No added inference latency; 4.7M trainable parameters for GPT-3 175B.
results.quote: This approach reduces the number of trainable parameters by 10,000× and reduces GPU memory requirements by 3× compared to GPT-3 175B fine-tuned with Adam

results.claim: The survey's own comparative tables (6, 7) are narrative restatements of each paper's headline numbers, not a re-measurement on common hardware or models.
results.setup: Tables 5, 6, 7 compare techniques on performance, cost, scalability using each source paper's reported setup.
results.note: Inferred from the table contents; the paper does not state this.

limits: Authors concede: timeframe 2017 to December 2023 only; search queries may miss other terminology; database coverage may miss relevant studies (Sec XI).
All numbers are quoted from the original papers under differing hardware, models and baselines; the survey does not normalise them, and several baselines are unnamed.
Some figures are inconsistent or garbled (FlexGen 69x vs 79x; GPTQ speedup sentence; Li et al sequence-parallelism row has a missing multiplier).

Speculative decoding, continuous batching, FlashAttention, KV-cache quantization, MLA and prefix caching are absent; the corpus stops at December 2023, so 2024-2026 serving work has dated this survey.
Search used AI screening tools (Rayyan, ResearchRabbit); selection of the final 65 from 195 assessed is only loosely specified (130 'focus on different aims').
Several summaries conflate training and inference (PagedAttention listed under training optimization; LightSeq2 listed as serving).
Text says last search 25 May 2024 but the window ends December 2023, and the template still reads IEEE Access vol 11, 2023.
practices: Use hybrid CPU/GPU/NVMe offloading (FlexGen, DeepSpeed ZeRO-Inference) when a model does not fit in GPU memory and throughput matters more than latency (Sec IV-B1, IV-B2).
Split prompt computation and token generation across differently provisioned machines to trade cost, throughput and power (Splitwise, Sec IV-B9).
Use block-based KV-cache management (PagedAttention) to reduce fragmentation and share cache across requests (Sec IV-C1).
Apply post-training quantization to 3-4 bits (GPTQ) or W4A8 (FPTQ) for single-GPU inference of very large models (Sec V-B1).
Apply one-shot pruning (SparseGPT) at about 50% sparsity on very large models, which tolerate pruning better than small ones (Sec V-B2).
Batch variable-length requests with a sequence-length-aware scheduler and allocator (TurboTransformers, Sec IV-B4).
Future work: dynamic quantization that adjusts precision at run time, adaptive parallelism, resource-aware scheduling (Sec X).
Hot/cold neuron placement across GPU and CPU for consumer-GPU inference (PowerInfer, Sec IV-B11).
